examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Third-Degree Taylor Polynomial For a Given Function About a Given Point
examples.problem: Find the third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x) = \ln(1+x)$ about $x=0.$
examples.worked_solution:
To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
P_3(x) = f(0) + f'(0)(x-0) + \dfrac{1}{2!}f''(0)(x-0)^2 + \dfrac{1}{3!}f'''(0)(x-0)^3.
$$

We need to compute $f(0),$ $f'(0),$ $f''(0),$ and $f'''(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+0)=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =(1+x)^{-1} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =(1+0)^{-1}=1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-(1+x)^{-2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =-(1+0)^{-2}=-1 \\ {f}^{(3)}(x) & =2(1+x)^{-3} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(0) & =2(1+0)^{-3}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f(0),$ $f'(0),$ $f''(0),$ and $f'''(0)$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =0+(1)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2!}(-1)(x-0)^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}(2)(x-0)^{3} \\  & =x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Let $f(x)$ be a function with $f(4)=1,{f}^{′}(4)=-1,{f}^{″}(4)=-2$ and ${f}^{‴}(4)=12.$ Which of the following is the third-degree Taylor polynomial for $f(x)$ about $x=4?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(4)+{f}^{′}(4)(x-4)+\frac{{f}^{″}(4)}{2!}(x-4)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(4)}{3!}(x-4)^{3} \\  & =f(4)+{f}^{′}(4)(x-4)+\frac{{f}^{″}(4)}{2}(x-4)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(4)}{6}(x-4)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We have been given the following set of values: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =-1 \\ {f}^{″}(4) & =-2 \\ {f}^{‴}(4) & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given values into our Taylor polynomial, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =1-1(x-4)+\frac{(-2)}{2}(x-4)^{2}+\frac{12}{6}(x-4)^{3} \\  & =1-(x-4)-(x-4)^{2}+2(x-4)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
